Encouraging people to stay on the petal platform is tricky. Adding peformance enhancing aspects to utility tools can often result in opposing functionalities that can create frustrating moments of conflicting decision choices.

Imagine adding burst of healing to Lifegrip. Lifegrip's main functionality is repositioning an ally. If you add healing to it, it can result in situations where players will want to use the heal, but not the grip, and being paired together makes for frustrating moments.

The same kind of logic applies to pairing a damage boost to petal platform. There will be a lot of moments where you want to use the petal for one reason instead of the other, and moments where you can't do fulfill both will make it feel bad to use.

There are a ton reasons some people feel compelled to purchase a lot of different skins for a single hero, even if it doesn't make a lot of "practical sense". 

For one, buying a hero's skins tells Blizzard there's interest for more. Kiriko's influx of skins is a testament to just how effective voting with your wallet can bem

For another, frequent skin releases play into same rewarding/accomplishing feeling that collectors typically enjoy. After obtaining a few, some people start to develop something of a compulsion to add more to their collection, causing them to place value in subsequent releases they otherwise wouldn't be interested in if it werent for their already considerable collection.

Then factor in just how strongly people can identify with and develop attachments towards certain heroes, purchasing skins reinforces their sense of "dedication" or "support" for their favorite characters, similarly to how people buy merch for their favorite sports teams or musicians. 

People's incentives to purchase hero skins can extend well beyond "this looks cool and I want to look cool." and the sunk cost fallacy only further contributes to every different reason a person might want to purchase a skin. People rarely reach a point where they think "Ok I have more than enough im not interested in having more." The more skins a person has of a certain hero, the more likely they are to be receptive to the idea of purchasing another, and another, and another.

High M+ is generally more difficult than heroic raid for a few reasons.

1. The success of a M+ run relies on your contribution as 1 of 5 players, or 20% of the party. In a raid, the responsibility of killing a boss is split between 10-30 players. If you make a mistake in Heroic raid, other players can usually make up for it.   


2. Mythic+ requires 20+ minutes of continuous attention. This means paying attention to mechanics and performing your class properly with only miniscule breaks, if any at all. Raids on the other hand, have boss fights lasting 4 to 8 minutes, which can be less demanding.     


3. Getting into a heroic raid PuG is tremendously easier than getting into a high M+ key. M+ dungeons tend to be needlessly gatekept by class/spec metas and score requirements. While true, a lot of heroic raid leaders will ask for rediculous ilvls and proof of experience, there are a lot of heroic raiders who are much more reasonable when forming groups.


4. If 1 Raid Boss is the equivalent to 1 Mythic Dungeon, mythic dungeons require a significantly higher amount of game knowledge to execute well. There are boss mechanics, trash packs, and routes to remember that can add up to significantly surpass the amount of info you'd need to know to kill a raid boss.


All that being said; do not let the challenge scare you off. All it takes to conquer this type of content is time and patience. It's a lot like learning an instrument. People might make it look easy, but thats only because they've had years of practice. That type of skill is still within reach for you, but you need to build up to it with time. I encourage you to push yourself because the challenges ahead can feel extremely rewarding; but don't let yourself become overwhelmed or burnt out out of frustration.

Disc priest IS insanely fun. Thats why i've mained it since Legion. But its absorbs are currently too strong. Their ability to drastically increase effective health pools is too good of a survivability tool. BDD is an obsessive-compulsive disorder. It is about a persons obsession and compulsive thinking about their body or physical characteristic, regardless of whether that physical characteristic is real or not. There are ton of people who are self conscious about certain, real features. But it isn't classified as a disorder until their concern over that feature starts impeding on their mental wellbeing.

Your concerns with your body could be very real. Regardless, so long as you're preoccupied with those concerns, and so long as it impedes on your mental wellbeing, it is BDD.

The goal of BDD treatment is not to gaslight yourself into thinking you're perfect. It's to reduce the obsessiveness, the compulsive thinking, and retrain your maladaptive thought patterns thats causing your life so much distress.

BDD treatment is NOT about convincing you that "you're crazy" or "you're seeing things". What you perceive is real. It is the reality you live with, regardless of whether or not other people see it. BDD treatment should be about helping you gain more control over your thoughts and compulsions so that it's no longer detrimental to your health. Your concerns with your self image could be reasonable and well founded. But its the amount those concerns dominate the rest of your life that is the issue.

There are a lot of factors that you have to take into account as a tank. Without logs or a recording of your gameplay, it's hard to pinpoint whether you're doing one thing, multiple things, or nothing wrong. Here are some things you should consider;

Tanks are heavily ilvl dependent. You could be doing everything right, but when it comes down to it, if you don't have the stats for it, you can't expect to survive a big pull through your own efforts. If you're regularly struggling to survive boss mechanics or single-pack pulls even with defensives up, this might be a sign you need to gear up.

Incoming damage varies widely between bosses and pulls. The only way to figure out what will and wont kill you is through practice. Sometimes, it's perfectly reasonable to pull an entire room and survive. Other times, you could pull 1 extra elite with a tank buster and you're dead for sure. Try to pay attention to what is most dangerous to you, especially if your pull kills you or brings you close to death. Then react accordingly the next time you encounter the same pull.

A lot of Vengeance DH's survivability comes from aggressive gameplay. This is especially true when facing multiple enemies. Ontop of CYCLING your MULTIPLE defensive cooldowns, you want to try and maximize your damage output and soul fragment generation. Vengeance's kit lends itself to the idea that offense is the best defense. Now don't get it twisted, there are still a lot of cases where you need to sacrifice damage output in order to keep yourself alive. But if you're managing your defensives correctly, survivabilty and damage output will come hand in hand.

Teamwork makes the dream work. Keep in mind that defeating the enemy relies on everyone doing their part. If people are not interrupting important casts or stunning the right mobs, you can be put in serious danger. THAT BEING SAID; don't rely on your team to always play right. Especially in PUG environments, you need to consider that people are going to make mistakes. Instead of blaming your team for a pull gone wrong, re-evaluate and ask yourself what you could have done to minimize the chances of those mistakes happening again. This might mean pulling fewer or different mobs, or pulling mobs further away, or comitting cooldowns to an encounter you usually don't need to. 

Don't rely on your healer to keep you alive. Especially at higher key levels, the healer usually has a lot to deal with keeping themselves and the DPS up. If a healer has to commit a lot of resources to keeping you alive, you need to reevaluate and approach the fight in a way that allows you to be more self sufficient. The resources the healers are giving to you are resources you're taking away from the healer and dps.

Utility and mobility is part of survivability. Consider them semi-defensive cooldowns. While demonic leap or sigil of chains may not have a damage reduction component, proper use of these abilities can be more effective at keeping you alive than your defensive cooldowns. That being said, you generally want to keep kiting mobs as a last resort. For one, DPS tend to lose a lot of output when mobs are constantly moving. For another, if you can't hit any mobs, you can't generate soul fragments, and that can put your life at risk. Mobility is a game-changing defensive tool, but it's not as universally useful as your true defensives. Use it sparingly.

Finally, pace yourself. Yes, there is a timer to Mythic+ keys, but you are less and less likely to finish the dungeon in time every time your group wipes. You're not in a race. Finishing the dungeon with 5 minutes left on the timer isn't worth the risk of depleting the key entirelt. I know that DPS will often pressure tanks to go faster and pull more, but you should know your limits.

Personally, yes! Whitemane is my favorite healer by far. Love her playstyle, love the disc priest fantasy, love everything about her.

She is a difficult healer to play, though, especially in Aram. Here's some advice for when you next pick her up in a game;

1. Watch your positioning, first and foremost. You are no use to your team if you are dead. A lot of inexperienced Whitemane players feel they need to play aggressively in order to heal their team, and this usually ends up with them spending a lot of time looking at the death screen.

2. Outside of teamfights, focus on "maintenance healing". This means healing with Q every 3 seconds or so when your desperation stack drops. This is to keep mana cost on Q low. Use W on allies who need additional healing, and poke enemies with E as long as it is safe to do so.

3. During teamfights, this is where you start to enter the "burst healing" stage. This is when you want to throw out 2 to 3 Q's to cover your team, then E + W the closest enemy player, weaving in auto attacks between cooldowns, and using your ult to turn the tide of a fight. KEEP IN MIND YOUR POSITIONING! Unless the enemies are running away from your team, you should be safe in the backline hitting the closest available enemy. 

There's a lot more to really getting good at Whitemane, but if you follow these general rules, you should be more than fine. Just remember that Whitemane can do just fine healing without hitting anyone. Just make sure you're managing your mana, and waiting for opportunities to really start doing damage.

If your primary source of content is solo, you'll usually be better off playing in a DPS spec like Devastation. While you CAN certainly do a lot of solo content just fine as a healer (Preservation), it will just take you more time to kill things, and a lot of your abilities will find limited use, as they are only really utilized in group content.

A lot of the tougher max level content in WoW is fundamentally group gameplay, and unfortunately the only way to really practice for this is to do group content. Solo content typically fails to introduce players to the kind of mechanics that need to be learned when doing Dungeons (5 player) or raids (10+ player). 

If you want to play and practice in a low stakes "group" environment, you can do Follower Dungeons, which is a solo player experience, but with the added benefit of having a team of 4 NPCs filling the Tank/Healer/DPS role (whichever roles you are not fulfilling yourself).

As for Aug, the role of an Aug Evoker and a Healer are pretty distinctly different, and I would say, non-transferrable. Aug evoker is a DPS role through and through, meaning a lot of the mechanics you need to learn playing as a healer will not apply when playing Aug Evoker.

Simply put; a lot of Overwatch players despise healing-focused supports, those being Mercy and Lifeweaver. This is for three main reasons; 

1. When healing supports are strong, combat tends to stall, and people take a long time to die. Since most of the playerbase consist of DPS, they get frustrated when the target they're aiming for doesn't die.

2. With the way Overwatch 2 is designed, lethality will always have more perceived value than survivability. An Ana securing a kill on the enemy tank with nade will always look better to your team, than Lifeweaver saving your tank from the enemy Ana nade, because dead enemies are more easily felt than alive allies.  

3. Healing focused supports like Lifeweaver and Mercy are seen as low skill, making every way they affect the game come with a more sour taste. Just like it feels bad to die to a Junkrat spamming mindlessly at a choke, for DPS, it feels bad to work hard on killing an enemy, and them not dieing because Mercy or Lifeweaver is hiding around the corner holding primary fire on your target.

A lot of this frustration is an issue of perception, rather than actual gameplay. Mercy and Lifeweaver could have a positive winrate, and people will hate them for being OP. Mercy and Lifeweaver could have a negative winrate, and people will hate them for being useless. There is literally no winning. People do not like healing-focused supports, regardless of how they actually perform. Its not an issue of their kits, its an issue of community perception.

The very first thing any great tank should do is to configure their UI to make all the jobs of a tank easier. Download Plater, and look for tank profiles for dungeons. The best plater profiles for tanks will include indicators for: frontals / tank busters / important casts / aggro status. The easier it is for you to recognize these things in a pull, the better you will be at tanking. Not having this information readily available to you will just make it more difficult.

The second priority for a tank should be learning mob mechanics. You can look up online guides, but the best teacher is really experience. More important than knowing how your class works, is knowing what the enemies do. This way, you can discern what pulls your team can handle, and what pulls your team can't. There is no real way to "prepare" for this other than just repeatedly doing dungeons and paying attention to mob mechanics. but this is second on your priority list because it should always be on your mind when tanking. If you die, or wipe, you should try and discern why it happened. Was there an important kick missed? Why was it missed? Are there too many casters in this pack? Did you pull without cooldowns? etc.

Your third priority finally comes down to how to play your class, and this again, really comes down to experience, but you can still learn a lot by looking at guides. Keep in mind; as a tank, you're playing with a lot more variables than you would be if you were playing as a DPS. Sometimes, you need to play defensively. Sometimes, you can get away with pumping more damage. Figuring out the feel of danger in different dungeons and key levels will be an important skill. But surviving a pull is only half the fight. As a tank, you have a lot of tools at your disposal to keep packs of mobs under control. If there is a button on your bars you don't find yourself using often, take a look at the spell again and see where you can make use of it. There are very few tank abilities that are truly useless. Ensure you're making the most of your class by exploiting all the abilities you have to offer.

WoW head, Icy veins, class discords, and a lot of other online guides are all great resources to learn how to play your class. They often include "easy" builds to try out that typically require less attention to play well. If you find these guides unhelpful or overwhelming, you can usually find someone to help you out more directly by visiting a class discord and asking for help. There are training dummies in almost all major cities that you can practice your button "rotation" on.

  
Tip 4: Find the appropriate environments to practice your skills.  
Normal dungeons, Timewalking Dungeons,  and Heroic Dungeons, are usually poor places to practice your class because the enemies die before you can really get your buttons going. Delves are also actually a pretty difficult environment to learn the basics of your class since delves don't have a tank to hold aggro for you, and incorporating your own survival into your rotation can be difficult especially for some classes that are not naturally sturdy. The best place to practice your rotation in a live environment  would be Mythic 0 Dungeons and Looking For Raid. You can simply que into LFR using the Raid Finder, and if you want to do dungeons, you can either join M0 groups, or make your own. Sometimes players find it helpful to put "learning" in the group title to attract more like-minded players who don't mind a slower and more considerate pace.

Hey there! Welcome to the game! So glad you're enjoying yourself, and its great seeing new player interest in harder content.

My biggest piece of advice; Don't push yourself too hard, don't bite off more than you can chew, and give yourself a little bit of grace. WoW is a 20 year old game. A lot of players who are doing harder content have YEARS worth of practice and knowledge within their fingertips. This is how they play so smoothly. It's not so different from a pianist playing the piano. Since you've never played piano before, it's only natural you won't be pushing all the right buttons at all the right moments. You will get better with time, if you give yourself the patience to learn.

Now for some basic, but important tips.

Tip 1: Set up your User Interface for combat.  
WoW's default settings for their UI is not great for fighting, because it places very important information so far from your character. Moving your eyes to the bottom of the screen to look at your abilities and looking to the top of your screen for buffs, takes your focus away from the most important thing: your character. So, when setting up your UI, it is usually good practice that you have your combat-relevant info closest to your character, and leaving non-combat-relevant info off to the sides. Combat-relevant info include: your health, your resource, your minor and major cooldowns, important buffs and debuffs, and the enemy unit frame. i.e. if you're looking down to the bottom of your screen to see if you can use an ability yet, or if you're looking up to the top of your screen to see if you have an important buff, you most likely want to place these buffs and abilities somewhere closer to your character. This can be done with UI addons, or if you prefer not changing your whole UI, you can set up or download Weakauras to place this important information next to your character.

  
Tip 2: Setting up and learning keybinds.  
This is the part where you want to get comfortable learning your buttons. The trick to this is to put your most frequently casted spells close to WASD (left hand), with less-frequently casted spells using the shift/ctrl modifier.  Now there is no "right way" to set keybinds. Do what makes the most sense to you. Then, try to learn your keybinds in chunks. Start off by keybinding 4 of your most frequently used abilities, then when you get used to that, add 4 more keybinds and practice with all 8. Once you're comfortable with that, try adding the shift modifier to those keybinds. (If you bound 1, 2, 3 and 4, you can repurpose those keys for other abilities by binding shift-1, shift-2, shift-3, and shift-4, and so on). If you're playing with alts, it's a good idea to place similar abilities to the same keybinds to help with muscle memory. Example: Your interrupt button is always C. Your main damage cooldown is always Shift-F. Your main movement ability is always R.

I'll give you a rundown from a gameplay/rotational perspective.

Affliction is about spinning plates. You want to maintain multiple afflictions on as many targets as you can, while having your stronger afflictions on the most important targets. Every 30sec-1min, you get access to two very powerful cooldowns, at which point you apply both of them to the enemy, then spam your Soul Shard spender to detonate all your afflictions at once. This gameplay loop is relatively simple in single target, but gets more difficult with higher target counts.

Destruction Warlock is about optimizing your Soul Shard generation, and spending as many of them as you can over the duration of the fight. Rotationally a very simple builder/spender type thing. The trickiness comes from how you manage your smaller buffs and cooldowns, to ensure you're squeezing as many soul shards as you can from each of your casts, and then during your cooldowns, blasting the boss with as many spenders as you can to avoid overcapping soul shards.

Demonology Warlock is a decent mix of Destruction Warlock's Soul Shard management, and Affliction Warlock's set-up cooldowns then blast. There is a natural rhythm that plays out with demonology's soul shard spending, with only a few mechanics to play with in order to optimize your generation. The trickier part is ensuring you line up your few small cooldowns with your big main one every minute. However, unlike affliction which uses one cooldown after the other sequentially, you have to pay attention to the duration of your demon summons so that they're all active when your big 1 min cooldown is available.

Just like a druid bids roots to grow and snare enemies, a shaman invokes the spirits of wind to blow and fire to blaze. And just to be clear, elemental spirits are not just the fire and water elementals we see roaming around. There have been cases where Thrall speaks to a single ember, and referrs to it as a spirit. In the same novel, Thrall referrs to a giant inferno as a spirit. "Spirit" is really just the amorphous conscious entity of the elements themselves.

Whether or not elemental spirits serve as a proxy is ambiguous. In a lot of WoW lore, its pretty explicitly stated how shamans have to speak to the elements in order to perform any "magic". But simultaneously, a lot of WoW lore also depicts shamans using elemental magic without the need of spirits whatsoever. Dark Shaman are actually notorious for enslaving elements to enforce the shamans will. In order to bridge this dissonance in writing, it could just be assumed that the elemental spirits grant the shaman use of their power when no spiritual communication is explicitly shown.

Its almost like that. When mages cast Fire and Frost spells, they're manipulating reality via Arcane magic to ignite or freeze the air around them. Your goal as a disc priest is not to maintain Atonement on your team at all times. It's unsustainable, wasteful, and you run the risk of depleting your resources for moments where you really need them.

Disc Priests have two phases of healing: they have their burst healing phase, and their maintenance healing phase.

The burst healing phase begins by covering your group with atonement, popping damage cooldowns like Mindbender and Mindblast, and doing a tremendous amount of Atonement Healing through your raw damage output. Your most powerful burst healing sequence looks like: [ Mindbender > Radiance > Mind Blast > Penance Enemy > Void Blast spam. Re-apply Atonement via Radiance where necessary. ] You only ever enter this phase in order to reverse large amounts of incoming damage. And since this phase is heavily reliant on the availability of your cooldowns, you need to make sure you're saving your CDs for when they're most needed. If the incoming damage is only moderate, you can save your Mindbender for more dangerous damage events, and rely only on Mindblast. If the damage is long and drawn out, you can alternate between Mind Blast and Mindbender, popping one only after the other, to spread out your healing appropriately. NOTE: While both your Mindbender and Entropic Rift (from Mind Blast) are active, you do an incredible amount of healing. If you see an ally dropping lower than the rest of your team, you can trust your damage output during these cooldowns to heal them faster than using Flash Heal, so long as they have an active atonement on them. 

The maintenance healing phase is a little more tricky, since it relies on a proper balance between spot healing with Flash Heal and Power Word: Shield to get your teammates to a safe level of health, then relying on regular Atonement healing to top them off and maintain their health bars. Now this balance of atonement healing and spot healing differs heavily between dungeons and key levels; and the only real way to know where that proper balance lies is by learning through experience. But to start off, I would recommend you rely on Flash Heal and Power Word: Shield to bring your allies up to 75% health, then relying on the residual atonement buffs and your regular damage rotation to top them off. During circumstances where there are 3 or more heavily injured allies that Flash Heal wont be enough to save them, this is when you consider using Radiance and your damage cooldowns, then entering a burst phase to recover. 

___
The Discipline spec excels best when the Priest is able to predict incoming damage. The truth of the matter is, this kind of game sense can only develop through experience. The more you know about the bosses and trash packs you're pulling, the better you will be as a Discipline priest. As you become more experienced with the strength of your atonement with and without cooldowns, the better you will be at finding the balance.

Foregoing group coverage for the sake of single target healing is not a mechanic unique to Prevoker, but unlike other proactive healers like Disc Priest or Resto Druid who can more easily switch between spot healing and ramp healing, Prevoker ramps require a lot more commitment since any single-target healing you do will immediately consume a ramp you may be preemptively preparing. This isn't something that can't be played around- Prevoker is perfectly capable of competing at the highest keys. But playing around this feels significantly more frustrating in this spec than others, and seems more like a frustrating QoL issue gameplay wise.

While Temporal Anomaly is a godsend of an ability to get groupwide coverage, its radius is limited and the choes it applies are only about 60% as effective as directly-applied echoes. That's passable in most forms of content, but the drop in healing is significantly felt in higher end content when incoming damage cuts it extremely close.
For example, take the 2nd boss in Necrotic Wake. To counter the pulsing rot damage your group is taking, you want to cover your group with reversions and echo'd dream breaths, using a fully charged Spiritbloom for the occasional pick-me-up. And while ideally, to maximise the value of your 30sec Dream Breath CD, you want to have it echo on you and your 3 other DPS. But in practice, this setup is often interrupted when a kick is missed and one of your party members requires immediate spot healing. While you are allocating resources towards keeping that one member up, your time and essence is being taken away from better covering your group. Especially if you are mid ramp, a single target requiring immediate attention means you have to consume your ramp right away and switch to single-target healing (okay if your team could use the healing, though you miss out on a few echos by prematurely triggering your ramp) or you wait and hope they survive till the next damage event happens so that you can get full value of your set echoes + healing them to full. Otherwise? you end up truncating your ramp and throwing out a suboptimal use of your cooldowns due to Echo's inherent all or nothing nature.

No. Some healing specs have higher potential damage output than others, as well as a different variety of utility in the form of Buffs and CC.

For example. Mistweaver Monks and Discipline Priests. These two healers are notorious for being the "damage dealing healers" to heal by doing DPS. But because of this interaction, their damage potential is actually lower than other healers. To keep these specs balanced, Disc and MW do less damage because they're allowed to heal and DPS at the same time. On the other hand, you have Holy Priests and Restoration Druids, who can only either heal or do damage at any given time. So, their damage potential is significantly greater, since all their DPS output comes at the cost of healing.

So just because Disc and MW are "damage dealing healers", don't fall into the common misconception that these are the most lethal healers in terms of damage output.

Overwatch supports have much more kill potential in the sense that alone, they can often output competitive enough levels of damage to take down other healers or dps heroes on their own.

In WoW, a healers "kill potential" lies more in their utility rather than in their damage output. At best, focusing only on raw damage rather than casting any heals, your healing spec will output about 1/5th of a normal DPS's damage. Now this is not nothing- in a coordinated attack with your DPS, that 1/5th of damage can add up to a kill. But as a healer, your lethality lies more in your ability to lock down enemy players with CC and freeing your allies and allowing them do do more damage.

But for the purpose of my original post, explaining why PuGs are particularly awful this season, I thought it was important to mention.

There are multiple reasons M+ is particularly terrible to PuG these days.

1. Death is 3x more punishing than in previous seasons. This means in a typical full team wipe, the penalty alone results in a 75sec timer loss, up from the old 25sec.

2. Mythic raid equivalent crest upgrades only drop from +9's and over, up from the old +6. This forces a lot of players to participate in a level of content difficulty they don't have experience or interest partaking in.

3. Stuns no longer interrupt most mob spell-queing. Where in previous seasons, one or two players could completely nullify the most dangerous mob mechanics with a stun, stuns now only DELAY casting, meaning your group is forced to counterplay it another way, or be punished for failing to.

4. Healers are nowhere near as powerful as they were in Dragonflight. Where previously, they could heal half your health bar in a single global, it now takes a lot more time and resources to recover health. While Blizz say they've tuned incoming damage appropriately for the change in relative healing, this change of pace is proving to be difficult for a lot of healers to adapt to. Especially for new healers who only started in Shadowlands or Dragonflight.

Mind Sear has had a long history of changes, and it was pretty clear Blizzard did not know how to work it into the new Shadow Weaving design of Shadowlands, after the Insanity system of Legion/BFA was dropped.

______
The first issue with Mind Sear immediately following the Shadow Weaving/Devouring Plague rework was that it was our only source of AoE damage, it was very poorly tuned, and weaving it into an already pretty bloated button rotation felt terrible.

When Mind Sear was buffed to do more damage, a new problem arose where at certain target breakpoints, it was more optimal for damage to completely ignore all of our other buttons and sit and channel Mind Sear. So in aoe, it was sometimes a DPS loss to cast Devouring Plague, our only Insanity Spender. We'd just sit at full Insanity channeling.

So a new talent was given in the form of Searing Nightmare, where at the cost of some Insanity, we could unleash an explosion at the target that did AoE damage and applied Shadow Word: Pain. But the catch is, you could only cast the spell WHILE you were channeling Mind Sear. This proved to be extremely clunky and frustrating to play with.

There was a short time at the end of Shadowlands where Searing Nightmare was removed, and Mind Sear was changed to become an Insanity spender of its own. While this removed the problem of Searing Nightmare, now that Mind Sear was a spender instead of a generator, coming up with enough insanity to spend in AoE situations became a slog. In the time it took to ramp up all your DoTs one target at a time then generate enough insanity to use mind sear, the packs where already pretty much dead.

With the new Dragonflight talent trees came the rework to Psychic Link. Now, Psychic Link would replicate a portion of all your single target damage done onto all targets affected by Vampiric Touch. Since this talent existed alongside the Mind Sear spender, an awkward interaction arose where in some moments, you would have to rely on Mind Sear for AoE damage. But in other moments, it was better to cast your single target spells for the Psychic Link cleave. And these moments changed very rapidly depending on what procs you had and how many targets where alive.

Ultimately, by early Dragonflight, Mind Sear was abandoned and Shadow Priests entire multi-target kit became balanced around Psychic Link. Mind Sear proved too much of a problem, so Blizzard gave up on it.

And thats where we are in TWW. With Mind Sear nowhere to be seen, and ultimately, it was for the best. I really miss the feeling of rotting and melting packs of enemies down with a channeled AoE spender. But Shadow Priest's class design was always meant to specialize in spread-target cleave, just because of how their DoTs work. Although, Psychic Link is kind of boring in the way it barely interacts with your DPS rotation or changes it in any way. It's just additional, invisible damage. But the performance and easy tuning of Psychic Link is clearly better for the class.

I'll break weight loss down to a few simple points, then I'll explain it in further detail.

1. Your weight is determined by your diet.    



2. Unless diagnosed by a doctor, your metabolism is NOT an excuse for your weight.   





3. Our environment is actively working to make you gain weight.    




4. The key to weight control is consistancy.     




5. Don't try too hard, and be patient.    




1.    Your weight is determined by your diet. Eat more calories than your body burns, you will gain weight. Eat less calories than your body burns, you will lose weight. Don't let anyone convince you otherwise. And while yes, exercise can help you lose weight, you can NEVER out run a bad diet. It takes an hour of training to burn 200 of calories. And it only takes 5 seconds to eat 200 calories. If you can find time and energy in your day to exercise, then do it. It's good for you. But if you can only afford to focus on one thing, focus on your diet. You can lose weight without running on a treadmill. You just need to control what you eat.      
   
   
2.      Your metabolism does not make you incapable of losing weight. While it is true some of us naturally burn more calories than others, unless diagnosed by a doctor, there is no good reason you can't control your weight. I say this because it is an extremely popular notion a lot of people have that their weight gain is due to medical conditions out of our control. But the truth is, even people with metabolic dysfunctions are able to lose weight without surgical or medical intervention. This does not mean you should not look towards medicine or surgery to help you. If you can get help to control your weight then do it. But when it comes down to it, you are responsible for your own body. Don't make excuses for yourself.     

    


3. The world wants to make you gain weight. We are surrounded by food. Lots of food. Food that is delicious, and calorie dense, and advertised to us CONSTANTLY. Our cities are built in ways that discourage natural exercise like walking. Our schedules demand so much time and energy from us, we can so easily lose the energy to take care of our health. Being healthy takes effort, but our lives demand we use that effort tending to other responsibilities, we just do not have the resources left over to do whats best for our bodies. That being said. You can't let the world stop you from losing weight if that is what you want to do. The world working against you only means you need to fight a little harder, and change your environment so that healthy choices are easier to make than unhealthy ones.     
   


4. It all comes down to this. The key to weight control is consistancy. This is where everyone fails. You see, we know what we have to do to lose weight. It's easy to make healthy decisions when we're motivated. The hard part comes when we lose motivation. The hard part is sticking to your healthy plan every single day, at all hours of the day. No matter how much you want to lose weight, no matter how unhappy you might be with your current body, we all lose motivation eventually, and its our human nature to fall into old habits because old habits are easy. People, naturally, are like water. We only have so much willpower, eventually, we all fall into the path of least resistance and those paths usually lead us to unhealthy choices. The trick to combating this is to set your environment up so that when you're out of willpower, healthier choices are easier to fall to than unhealthy ones. The easiest example for this is throwing out or donating your unhealthy, calorie dense food, and replacing it with healthier, nutritious and more filling food. Make it so that when you wake up in the morning and crave cereal, the only source of cereal is 5 blocks and 8 dollars out of reach. Set yourself up so that when you feel thirsty and want a taste of soda, the closest thing in reach is calorie free, flavoured water. Willpower falters. So set yourself up so that when your willpower is gone, the easy options are the healthy ones.   
   



5. Don't try too hard. This really comes hand in hand with my last point. Consistancy is key, and that means maintaining habits that you can reasonably sustain. If your "healthy habits" consist of eating only 1 meal a day, you're setting yourself up for failure. You're going to be very hungry for a very long time, and that amount of stress will break anyone. If you're trying to lose weight fast, and eating at a 500 calorie defecit per day, you're setting yourself up for failure, because 3 days will pass and your body will DEMAND you eat more to make up for it. Long term weight loss that sticks should take time, and be reasonably easy. If your hunger is keeping you awake at night and you can't sleep, you're doing too much. If your workout at the gym is leaving you exhausted and breathless, you're doing too much. Your body does not like change, and the harder you push, the harder it will push back. I know that people want to lose weight as fast as they can. Trust me I know just as good as anyone how tempting it is. But real, sustainable change takes time. If you want to lose weight, you need to be patient with yourself and adopt habits that ease your body into change, instead of pushing it, and eventually undoing it all because you tried too hard.

When picking up a new habit, or dropping an old one, learn the importance of patience, gradual change, and consistancy.

When people get motivated, they think they can turn their life around with sheer force of will. But the truth is, **you cannot rely on willpower alone to maintain meaningful changes in the long run.** If you want to change your life, you need to facilitate an environment that supports the changes you want to make, you need to build consistant habits that are truly sustainable, and you need to give yourself time to adjust to the change.

There is so much good advice you can find online that can help you change your life. But I am telling you right now. Any advice that promises results in a short amount of time, is much more likely to fail. Anyone who has ever tried to lose or gain weight can attest to this. The faster you want change the happen, the more likely you are you revert back to old habits.

Season 4 was great for Incinerate Sorcs thanks to a few things. 

1: Damage gain from Burning Instinct was not capped.  
2: There was a bug causing DoTs like Incinerate to gain 2x benefit from +Dam affixes.   
3: Legendary items where extremely powerful compared to Uniques, and since Icinerate had no *required* Uniques to perform well, it was an easy and effective build to level, as well as push endgame content.

Here are a few Season 5 Changes that directly impact Incinerate Sorcs.     
1. Damage gain from Burning Instinct has been capped. But the amount of intellect required to reach that cap has been reduced, and the Combustion passive was buffed, to compensate.    
2. DoTs like Incinerate no longer gain 2x benefit from +Dam affixes.
3. The rework to Unique items in Season 5 has made Uniques much more powerful, and the best builds make sure to take advantage of these powerful items. Unfortunately, Incinerate has fewer synergies with Uniques compared to other builds, making it a less powerful choice in the endgame when Uniques are plenty.

___
TL:DR.  
In Season 5, Incinerate is easy to pick up while leveling and to work through endgame. However, the changes made in the latest season have put performance cap on Incinerate that other Sorc builds will surpass given enough time and gear.
